top.line: A skill policy compares described, actual and granted mandates
top.para: A video's claim that 1 in 20 Claude skills hack you overstates a study finding 5.2% with patterns suggesting malicious intent. A skill behaviour policy compares what a skill promises, what it can do and what its environment grants, then generates a hook and sandbox setting. Run on 899 public skills, it found 39 undescribed features and none obfuscated.

in-short.line: The gaps between three mandates are the findings
in-short.para: The 5.2% figure came from 31,132 marketplace skills in one study. Findings are features, not verdicts, the grant depends on where a skill runs, and of 899 skills, 812 reach beyond their scripts and 39 have an undescribed feature. A scanner asks if a skill looks malicious; a policy asks what it needs.

claim.line: The 1-in-20 claim is marketplace skills suggesting intent
claim.para: The number comes from Agent Skills in the Wild, which analysed 31,132 skills and found 26.1% with a vulnerability and 5.2% with patterns suggesting malicious intent. It concerns marketplace skills, not Claude's own, and NVIDIA's SkillSpector did not produce it. Skills still run with implicit trust and minimal vetting.

three.line: Undescribed features are suspicious; unrequested grant is excess
three.para: Each skill has a described mandate, an actual mandate found in its instructions and files, and a grant set by its environment. On Claude Code skills get any program's network access; through the API, none. Claude Code's allowed-tools pre-approves rather than restricts, so a skill can widen its own grant.

features.line: Every finding is a feature, judged by its context
features.para: An upload could be exfiltration or a login, and reading ~/.claude could be harvesting or requested analysis. The policy records each feature as a row with what it does, why the description needs it, and whether the description says so. An unexplained feature is a finding.

measured.line: Of 899 skills, 812 reach beyond their own scripts
measured.para: A static calculator read skills from Anthropic's repository, obra/superpowers and ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills on 14 October. 782 reach out through one third-party tool server, and 39 have undescribed features such as installs or outside paths. None was obfuscated, but description and reach often differ even when everyone means well.

example.line: An honest lethal-trifecta skill still needs a control
example.para: developer-growth-analysis reads Claude Code chat history, searches HackerNews and posts to Slack, describing all but the server in between. Four policy rows produced a hook, tested on nine inputs, that allows the history file, denies SSH keys and .env, and asks before sending. Script network access belongs to the sandbox.

scanner.line: Scanners ask about malice; policies ask about need
scanner.para: NVIDIA's SkillSpector 2.12.0, run statically on five skills, rated developer-growth-analysis safe and gave connect and quickbooks-automation zero. Both tools flagged langsmith-fetch's ~/.bashrc key line. The scanner rightly says these mostly do not look malicious, while the policy shows what each needs, gets and must be limited to.

service.line: Skill policies can become a service and open format
service.para: For any skill, the service would state the described and actual mandates, the minimal grant, extra reach on Claude Code, claude.ai and the API, and tested hook and sandbox settings. The calculator is cheap and static, with a model for judgement. Chainguard's planned skill policies would need this written down.

limits.line: Pattern matching gives lower bounds; nothing is called malicious
limits.para: The calculator misses features it has no pattern for, and the 899 skills come from curated sources, not marketplaces. The hook was tested on fixed inputs only, and SkillSpector ran without its model stage on five skills. A feature remains a feature until context says otherwise.

sources.line: Sources: the skills study, SkillSpector and Anthropic docs
sources.para: Written from a 14 October 2026 voice memo, with skills read as text in an isolated folder and never run. Sources are Liu et al., Agent Skills in the Wild (January 2026), NVIDIA's SkillSpector and verified agent skills, and Anthropic's Claude Code skills, Agent Skills overview and sandboxing pages.
